title: BrickMedic — Find the missing connection
author: Jake Johnson
tracks: Agents That Act on Connected Data
description:
BrickMedic is a graph repair lab and MCP tool server for builders and AI agents working with small digital LEGO-style models. It finds assemblies with no path to the original base, proposes collision-free rigid translations, and verifies each candidate in a disposable FalkorDB graph. A 3D preview and the actual connection path explain each proposed action.

Eight typed MCP tools let an AI host import or inspect a model, plan repairs, test what disconnects if a brick is removed, recall memory, reject a placement, and apply a verified candidate when enabled. Plans, rejections, events and repair proofs persist in the graph. A real stdio test closes one client and reconnects a fresh client to continue the saved plan. Applying requires a current candidate ID and revision, repeats validation, and is disabled by default in MCP.

Every applied repair atomically stores a portable proof: complete before/after models, SHA-256 hashes, fixed anchors, translation, revision, connection counts and a base path. The independent verifier rebuilds both states in fresh FalkorDB graphs and rejects altered geometry or invented evidence.

Evidence: 35/35 synthetic models repaired; 114/114 proofs independently replayed; all original anchors preserved. The dataset is three demos plus 32 seeded generated tower builds, not a real-world or held-out benchmark. All 44 automated tests passed, including real FalkorDB integration and MCP handoff tests. Model, plan and rejection history also survived replacing the Docker container.

Includes responsive 3D/graph views, strict LDraw/JSON import, repaired-model export, complete local setup, a narrated walkthrough and a build article. Scope: up to 100 upright rectangular bricks/plates; stud connectivity, not physical strength. External MCP hosts bring their own model. The walkthrough uses deterministic graph mode; the optional Anthropic chooser has controlled-response tests but no verified live provider call.

Codex assisted with implementation, tests, documentation, article and demo preparation. Jake selected the project and directed its scope, graph rationale, release and submission.
falkor:
FalkorDB is the required primary database and decision boundary. Brick nodes hold geometry and original-anchor flags; reciprocal CONNECTED edges represent validated stud contacts and their stud counts. Parameterized Cypher traversals identify base-reachable bricks and loose components; shortestPath returns the evidence paths shown to the user and MCP host.

The planner enumerates bounded rigid translations after collision checks, writes each shortlisted candidate into a temporary graph, and queries reachability again. The proposed assembly must regain a path to an original anchor. Applying a current candidate rechecks the geometry and graph before updating the model. A counterfactual removal uses another isolated graph to find which OTHER previously anchored bricks lose all base paths, preserving the live revision. Trial graphs are deleted in finally blocks.

Model nodes persist snapshots, revisions and active plans. Rejection and Event nodes store placement memory and repair history. Repair nodes store replayable evidence with before/after hashes, revisions and full proofs, written atomically in the same Cypher operation as the repaired model. The verifier independently reconstructs both states and checks connection counts, preserved anchors and each path hop.

The same service backs the web app and eight typed MCP tools. Fresh MCP clients can recall a rejected placement and continue the same private session. Browser visitors have separate randomly named graphs. Per-session serialization and revision checks block stale/repeated applies within one writing process; shared sessions should use one writer at a time. Append-only storage in a named volume was verified across container replacement. If FalkorDB is unavailable, inspection and repair fail explicitly; there is no in-memory substitute.
positive: Cypher expresses the product's central questions directly: which bricks reach the original base, which disconnected bricks form one assembly, what path proves a repair, and what loses reachability after a removal. Separate graphs make candidate trials, independent proof replay and visitor isolation straightforward. Keeping repair memory and evidence alongside topology lets a fresh MCP client continue an earlier plan. The official TypeScript client and pinned Docker image made the full workflow reproducible.
improvements: More prominent shortestPath examples would help, including its WITH/RETURN placement and directed-traversal restriction. Reciprocal CONNECTED edges and WITH shortestPath resolved those issues here. Docker documentation could also make persistence configuration more explicit: this image's entrypoint uses REDIS_ARGS and FALKORDB_DATA_PATH rather than the Compose command override we initially tried. A compact TypeScript example covering trial-graph cleanup, persistent MCP handoffs, container-replacement tests and connection failures would be valuable.
